question: A user clicks **Preview**. Assume `showPreview()` exists, doesn't throw, and doesn't cancel the click. What happens?

snippets.code:
<form action="/save" method="post">
  <input name="title" value="Draft">
  <button onclick="showPreview()">Preview</button>
  <button type="submit">Save</button>
</form>

options.text: Only `showPreview()` runs; a `<button>` without a `type` does nothing by default
options.why: A `<button>` with a missing (or invalid) `type` is a submit button. Only `type="button"` makes it do nothing by default.

options.text: `showPreview()` runs, then the form is submitted to `/save`
The form is submitted immediately and `showPreview()` never runs
options.why: The click event (and its handler) is dispatched first. Submitting is the button's default activation behavior, which happens after the click event, unless a handler calls `event.preventDefault()`.

options.text: Nothing happens; only a button explicitly marked `type="submit"` can submit the form
options.why: A form can have several submit buttons, and any of them submits it. The clicked one becomes the "submitter" (its `name`/`value`, if any, are included in the form data).

explanation:
The `type` attribute of `<button>` defaults to `submit`, and so does any invalid value. So inside a form, a plain `<button>` is a submit button.

Clicking it dispatches the `click` event first (running `showPreview()`), then performs its default action: submitting the form. In practice, the preview flashes briefly and then the page navigates to `/save`. That is the symptom you would be debugging.

Fix: `<button type="button" onclick="showPreview()">`. Cancelling the click with `event.preventDefault()` also works. A good habit is to always write `type` on every `<button>`.

question: What's the state of these two controls when the page loads?

snippets.code:
<button disabled="false">Pay now</button>
<input type="checkbox" checked="false">

options.text: The button is enabled and the checkbox is unchecked
options.why: For boolean attributes the value is never read as true/false. The attribute is present, so it's on.

options.text: The button is disabled, but the checkbox is unchecked, because `checked` only works with the value `"checked"`
options.why: `checked` follows the same rule as `disabled`: presence means on. `checked`, `checked=""`, `checked="checked"` and even `checked="false"` all start the box checked.

options.text: It depends on the browser, because `"false"` is an invalid value
options.why: The value is technically non-conforming, but the spec defines the behavior precisely: only presence matters. All browsers agree.

options.text: The button is disabled and the checkbox is checked

explanation:
`disabled` and `checked` are boolean attributes: if the attribute is present, it's true; its value doesn't matter. The spec only allows an empty value or the attribute's own name (`disabled="disabled"`), but `"false"` still counts as present.

To turn one off, remove the attribute: `button.removeAttribute('disabled')`, or set the DOM property, which is a real boolean: `button.disabled = false`.

Checkboxes have one more detail. The `checked` attribute sets the *default* state and is reflected by `input.defaultChecked`. The `input.checked` property is the live state, so `input.checked = false` unchecks the box but leaves the attribute in place.

In JSX, `disabled={false}` works because React leaves the attribute out entirely.

question: All three scripts are external files, and all of them load successfully. Which statement about their execution order is guaranteed?

snippets.code:
<head>
  <script defer src="a.js"></script>
  <script async src="b.js"></script>
  <script defer src="c.js"></script>
</head>

options.text: `a.js` always runs before `c.js`; `b.js` may run before, between, or after them

options.why: Only `defer` scripts keep document order among themselves. An `async` script runs as soon as it finishes downloading, regardless of where it appears.

options.text: `b.js` always runs first, because `async` scripts don't wait for parsing
options.why: `async` scripts run when their download completes. If `b.js` is slow to download, parsing can finish and the deferred scripts can run first.

options.text: `a.js` and `c.js` run after the `load` event; `b.js` runs before it
options.why: Deferred scripts run after parsing finishes but **before** `DOMContentLoaded`, which fires before `load`. And `async` scripts also run before `load`, because `load` waits for them.

explanation:
- `defer`: downloads in parallel with parsing, runs after the document is fully parsed, **in document order**, before `DOMContentLoaded` fires.
- `async`: downloads in parallel and runs as soon as it's ready (pausing the parser if parsing isn't done yet). No ordering guarantee relative to other scripts, and it may run before or after `DOMContentLoaded`.

So the only guarantee here is that `a.js` runs before `c.js`. Note that `defer` and `async` have no effect on inline classic scripts (those without `src`).

question: A search box was pasted into a profile form. The user types in the search field and clicks **Search**. Later, on a fresh page load, they click **Save profile** instead. What happens in each case?

snippets.code:
<form id="profile" action="/profile" method="post">
  <input name="name">
  <form id="search" action="/search">
    <input name="q">
    <button>Search</button>
  </form>
  <button>Save profile</button>
</form>

options.text: **Search** submits `#profile` to `/profile` (with both `name` and `q`); **Save profile** does nothing
**Search** submits `#search` to `/search` with `q`; **Save profile** submits `#profile` to `/profile` with `name`
options.why: That assumes forms can nest. They can't: the parser ignores a `<form>` start tag while another form is open, so there is no `#search` element at all (`document.getElementById('search')` is `null`).

options.text: Both buttons submit `#profile` to `/profile`, because the inner `<form>` tag is ignored
options.why: Half right: the inner start tag is ignored. But the inner `</form>` end tag is not ignored. It closes the only open form, `#profile`, so **Save profile** ends up after the form, outside it.

options.text: The inner `<form>` start tag closes `#profile`, so **Search** submits `#search` with only `q`, and **Save profile** is outside any form
options.why:
A `
` start tag never closes an open form (unlike `
  • ` or `

    `). It is simply dropped, so the search field and button stay inside `#profile`.

explanation:
The parser keeps a "form element pointer" to the currently open form. Two rules apply here:

- A `<form>` start tag while that pointer is set is a parse error and is **ignored**. So `#search` is never created, and `q` and **Search** belong to `#profile`.
- A `</form>` end tag closes whatever form the pointer refers to. The inner `</form>` therefore closes `#profile`.

The resulting DOM:

```html
<form id="profile" action="/profile" method="post">
  <input name="name">
  <input name="q">
  <button>Search</button>
</form>
<button>Save profile</button>
```

Clicking **Search** submits `#profile` to `/profile` with `name` and `q`. **Save profile** has no form owner (`button.form === null`), so clicking it does nothing, and the last `</form>` is ignored as stray.

Fix: never nest forms. Put the search form outside the profile form, and if a control must sit visually inside another form, associate it with the right one using the `form` attribute, e.g. `<button form="search">`.

explanation:

- It's added to the **top layer**, so it paints above everything regardless of `z-index` or ancestors' `overflow`, and it gets a `::backdrop` pseudo-element that covers the viewport.
- Everything outside the dialog becomes **inert**: it can't be clicked, focused or tabbed to.

snippets.code:
<dialog id="a" open>A</dialog>
<dialog id="b">B</dialog>

<script>
  const attempt = (fn) => {
    try { fn(); return 'ok'; } catch (e) { return e.name; }
  };
  console.log(
    attempt(() => a.show()),
    attempt(() => a.showModal()),
    attempt(() => b.showModal()),
    attempt(() => b.showModal())
  );
</script>

options.why: This assumes `showModal()` can "upgrade" a non-modal dialog. It can't: `a` is already open non-modally (from the `open` attribute), and switching it to modal while open throws.

That was the behavior under the older spec, where `showModal()` threw on any open dialog. The current spec (and current browsers) make calling `showModal()` on a dialog that's already modal a harmless no-op.
Calling the **same** kind of open again is a no-op, not an error: `show()` on an already non-modal dialog and `showModal()` on an already modal dialog both just return.

explanation:
Both methods check whether the dialog is already open, and the result depends on whether the **mode** would change:
- `a.show()`: `a` is already open non-modally, so this returns without doing anything → `ok`.
- `a.showModal()`: `a` is open but **not** modal. The browser can't switch modes in place, so it throws `InvalidStateError`.
- `b.showModal()`: `b` was closed, so it opens modally → `ok`.
- `b.showModal()` again: already open **and** modal, so it returns → `ok`.

The mirror case also throws: `show()` on a dialog that's open modally is an `InvalidStateError`. (`showModal()` also throws if the dialog isn't connected to a document.)

In practice this bites when markup ships with `<dialog open>` and script later calls `showModal()`. Close it first, or don't use the `open` attribute at all:

```js
if (a.open && !a.matches(':modal')) a.close();
a.showModal();
```

- **When a `<details>` gets the `open` attribute** (user click, `el.open = true`, `setAttribute`): every other open element in the group is closed. So `q3.open = true` closes `q1`.

snippets.code:
<button id="cancelBtn">Cancel</button>
<form id="profile" inert>
  <input id="nick" value="Ann">
  <button id="save" type="button">Save</button>
</form>

<script>
  save.addEventListener('click', () => console.log('save clicked'));
  cancelBtn.focus();
  nick.focus();
  console.log(document.activeElement.id);
  save.click();
</script>

options.why: This treats `inert` as a pointer-only block, like `pointer-events: none`. Inert elements can't be focused at all, by Tab or by `focus()`, so `nick.focus()` does nothing.
This treats `inert` like `disabled`. Inert blocks **user** interaction (clicks, focus, selection, find-in-page) but not script: `element.click()` still dispatches a `click` event to an inert button.

options.text: An empty string (focus falls back to `<body>`), then `save clicked`
options.why: A `focus()` call on an element that can't be focused is simply ignored. It doesn't blur the element that currently has focus, so focus stays on Cancel.

explanation:
`inert` makes an element and its whole subtree behave as if the user can't reach it:
- it can't be focused (Tab skips it and `focus()` is ignored),
- real clicks go through it as if it weren't there (hit testing ignores it),
- its text can't be selected and it's hidden from assistive technology.

So `nick.focus()` is a no-op and focus stays on `cancelBtn`.

But `inert` is about **user** interaction only. It doesn't disable controls (`save.disabled` is still `false`, and it doesn't match `:disabled`), and a scripted `save.click()` still fires the listener. If a keyboard shortcut or other code calls `click()` or `submit()`, guard that code yourself, or disable the button as well:

```js
profile.inert = true;
save.disabled = true; // also blocks save.click()
```

Note that `inert` adds no visual styling. Dim the content yourself so users know it's unavailable.

question: `logo.png` is 200×50, `logo@2x.png` is 400×100 and `logo@3x.png` is 600×150. With an empty cache, which file is the best fit (and the one the browser requests) on a laptop with a device pixel ratio of 1, and on a phone with a device pixel ratio of 2?

options.text: `logo.png` on both: without a `1x` entry the `srcset` is ignored
options.why: A `srcset` doesn't need a `1x` entry to be used. The candidates are still valid; the browser just has one more candidate to choose from (the `src`).

options.text: `logo.png` on the laptop, `logo@2x.png` on the phone
`logo@2x.png` on both: `srcset` overrides `src`, and the lowest-density candidate in it is used at DPR 1
options.why: `srcset` doesn't throw the `src` away. When `srcset` uses x descriptors and has no `1x` entry, the `src` joins the candidate list as the `1x` candidate, which is the exact match at DPR 1.

options.text: `logo.png` on the laptop, `logo@3x.png` on the phone: high-density screens get the sharpest file
options.why: The browser picks the candidate that fits the screen's density, not the highest one. At DPR 2 the `2x` file is an exact fit; the `3x` file would just waste bandwidth.

explanation:
An x descriptor says how many image pixels map to one CSS pixel. The browser compares those densities with the device pixel ratio and picks the best fit.

- When `srcset` uses x descriptors (no `w`) and has no `1x` entry, the `src` is added as the `1x` candidate. So the candidates here are `logo.png` (1x), `logo@2x.png` (2x) and `logo@3x.png` (3x).
- DPR 1: `logo.png` is the exact fit. DPR 2: `logo@2x.png` is the exact fit (and a DPR 3 screen would get `logo@3x.png`).

The chosen file is displayed at its density-corrected size: the 400px-wide `logo@2x.png` used as a `2x` candidate is drawn 200 CSS pixels wide, the same as `logo.png` on the laptop. That's why x descriptors fit fixed-size images such as logos and icons.

The spec lets browsers weigh other factors (bandwidth, a cached higher-density file, zoom), which is why the question asks for the best fit with an empty cache.

question: The viewport is 1000px wide, the device pixel ratio is 1, and the cache is empty. Which file is the best fit (and the one the browser requests)?

options.text: `photo-640.jpg`: the more specific `(min-width: 900px)` condition gives a 600px slot
options.why: `sizes` isn't resolved by specificity like a CSS cascade. The browser takes the first entry whose media condition matches, and `(min-width: 600px)` comes first and already matches at 1000px.

options.text: `photo-1280.jpg`: like CSS, the last matching entry wins, and `100vw` always matches
options.why: That's how later CSS rules override earlier ones, but `sizes` is a list read left to right that stops at the first match. The final `100vw` is only a fallback for when no condition matches.

options.text: `photo-640.jpg`: the `src` is used because the `sizes` conditions overlap
options.why: Overlapping conditions are fine; they're simply checked in order. With `w` descriptors the `src` isn't even a separate candidate here.

explanation:
The browser reads `sizes` from left to right and uses the first entry whose media condition is true. An entry without a condition (here `100vw`) is the fallback.

At a 1000px viewport, `(min-width: 600px)` matches first, so the slot is 300px. The smallest candidate that covers 300 pixels at DPR 1 is `photo-320.jpg` (320 / 300 ≈ 1.07x). The `(min-width: 900px)` entry is never reached for any viewport, because every viewport that's at least 900px wide is also at least 600px wide.

With `min-width` conditions, put the widest breakpoint first:

```html
sizes="(min-width: 900px) 600px,
       (min-width: 600px) 300px,
       100vw"
```

With that order, a 1000px viewport gets a 600px slot and `photo-640.jpg`, and a 700px viewport gets a 300px slot and `photo-320.jpg`.

options.why: The `width`/`height` attributes are presentational hints, so any author CSS beats them. `height: auto` overrides `height="900"`, and `width: 100%` overrides `width="1600"`.

The ratio is available before a single byte of the image arrives: - `width: 100%` makes the box 400px wide (CSS beats the `width` attribute). - `height: auto` then follows the aspect ratio: 400 × 900 / 1600 = **225px**. The space is reserved up front, so nothing shifts when the image loads. The `auto` keyword means that once the image loads, its own natural ratio is used if it has one, so a slightly wrong attribute pair doesn't distort the photo. That's why the modern advice is to always set `width` and `height` to the image's real pixel dimensions (or any pair with the same ratio) and let CSS handle the responsive sizing with `max-width: 100%` or `width: 100%`, plus `height: auto`.

options.text: A lazy image is only fetched once layout shows it's near the viewport, so the hero request no longer starts early during parsing. It waits for the CSS and layout.
Lazy images wait for the user's first scroll, so the hero doesn't load until the visitor scrolls the page.

question: The clip has a soundtrack, but it's meant as a muted background loop. It autoplays on the developer's machine, but in Chrome with a fresh profile it doesn't start, and on an iPhone it doesn't play inline in the page. What's the fix?

snippets.code: Ship faster

options.text: Add `controls`: browsers only allow autoplay when the user can pause the video.
options.why: Showing controls has no effect on the autoplay policy. A video with sound and `controls` is still blocked from autoplaying, and a muted one autoplays without controls.

options.text: Write `autoplay="true"`: a bare `autoplay` attribute is ignored by Chrome.
options.why: `autoplay` is a boolean attribute: its presence turns it on, whatever the value. `autoplay="true"` behaves exactly like bare `autoplay`, and it's still blocked while the video has sound.

options.text: Add `muted` and `playsinline`: `<video src="/media/loop.mp4" autoplay muted loop playsinline>`

options.why: Script-started playback follows the same policy. Without a user gesture, `play()` on a video with sound returns a promise that rejects with `NotAllowedError`. Muting it first is what makes it allowed.

explanation:
Browsers block autoplay **with sound** until the user has shown interest in the site. Muted autoplay is allowed.

- **Chrome**: muted autoplay is always allowed. Autoplay with sound is allowed only in some cases, e.g. after the user has interacted with the site (a click or tap) or when Chrome's Media Engagement Index shows they often play media there. That's why it works on the developer's machine and fails in a fresh profile. The blocked video just stays paused, with no error from the `autoplay` attribute.
- **iPhone (Safari)**: a video only plays inline if it has `playsinline`; without it, playback happens in fullscreen, so a background loop can't autoplay in the page.

So a background video needs `autoplay muted playsinline` (plus `loop` if it should repeat).

Without `controls`, the browser shows no play/pause UI. For moving content that runs longer than 5 seconds, add your own pause button (WCAG 2.2.2) so the motion can be stopped.

question: An accessibility audit flags this chart, which the team made for a report. Which fix is correct?

options.text: Move `
options.why: A `<figcaption>` may be either the first or the last child of `<figure>`, so its position is fine. Moving it doesn't give the image any text alternative.

options.text: Add `alt=""`, because the `<figcaption>` already describes the image.
options.why: `alt=""` marks the image as decorative, and assistive technology then skips it entirely. The caption only names the chart; it doesn't say what the data shows, so screen reader users would lose the content.

options.text: Nothing: HTML allows omitting `alt` on an image inside a `<figure>` with a `<figcaption>`, so the audit is a false positive.
options.why: That exception exists only for images whose content the author can't know, such as user uploads on a photo-sharing site, and the spec says to keep those cases to an absolute minimum. The team made this chart, so it can and must describe it.

options.text: Add an `alt` that conveys what the chart shows, e.g. `alt="Bar chart: sales roughly doubled from Q1 to Q4"`, and keep the `<figcaption>` as the visible caption.

explanation:
`<figcaption>` and `alt` do different jobs:

- `alt` is the image's **text alternative**: what someone who can't see it needs to know. Without it the image has no accessible name, and a screen reader may announce just "image" or the file name.
- `<figcaption>` is a **caption** for the whole `<figure>`, visible to everyone. It labels the content; it doesn't replace it.

The spec says a caption is generally not suitable as replacement text, so don't copy the caption into `alt` either. Describe the information the image carries.

Other `<figure>` facts worth knowing:

- `<figcaption>` must be the first or last child of the `<figure>`.
- `<figure>` isn't just for images. It's for self-contained content referenced from the main text, such as code listings, diagrams, quotes or tables, that could be moved (e.g. to an appendix) without breaking the flow.

question: A legacy promo page shows a navy banner across the top half of the viewport. A developer adds `<!doctype html>` as the very first line, and the banner disappears: `.hero` is now `0` pixels tall. Why?

options.text: In standards mode an element with no content always collapses to a height of `0`, whatever its `height` says
options.why: Tempting because empty divs often look like they vanish, but that's only when their height is `auto`. An empty `<div>` with `height: 200px` or `height: 50vh` keeps that height in standards mode. The problem here is that `50%` can't be resolved.

options.text: In standards mode a percentage `height` is resolved against the parent's **width**, the way percentage padding is
options.why: That rule belongs to percentage `padding` and `margin`, which use the containing block's width. A percentage `height` uses the containing block's height, and when that height is `auto` (as `<body>`'s is here) the percentage behaves as `auto`.

options.text: Without a doctype the page ran in quirks mode, where a percentage height skips over `auto`-height ancestors and resolves against the viewport. In standards mode, `50%` of `<body>`'s `auto` height behaves as `auto`, so the empty div is `0` tall
Anything before `<html>` counts as page content, so the doctype pushes the `<style>` element out of `<head>` and its rules stop applying
options.why: The doctype is a separate token that only selects the rendering mode; it doesn't create content or move elements. The styles still apply: after the change, `getComputedStyle(hero).backgroundColor` is still `rgb(0, 0, 128)`. It's the computed height that is `0px`.

explanation:
A missing (or old, unrecognized) doctype puts the document in **quirks mode**, which you can see in the console: `document.compatMode` is `"BackCompat"` without the doctype and `"CSS1Compat"` with `<!doctype html>`.

Quirks mode keeps old layout bugs for compatibility. One of them is the **percentage height quirk**: if the parent's height is `auto`, a percentage height is resolved against the nearest ancestor that has a definite height, up to the viewport. In an 800px-tall viewport, `.hero` was 400px tall in quirks mode.

In standards mode, a percentage height needs a containing block with a definite height. `<body>` and `<html>` both have `height: auto`, so `50%` behaves as `auto`, and an empty block with `auto` height is 0px tall.

Fixes for standards mode:
- Give the chain a definite height: `html, body { height: 100%; }`.
- Or size against the viewport directly: `.hero { height: 50vh; }`.

Quirks mode changes other layout details too (for example, an image alone in a block usually has no gap below it). Always start pages with `<!doctype html>` and fix the layout in standards mode instead of relying on quirks.

question: In a narrow desktop window this page switches to the one-column layout. On a phone about 390 CSS pixels wide it shows the full desktop layout shrunk down, and the media query never applies. What's missing?

snippets.code:
<!doctype html>
<html lang="en">
<head>
  <meta charset="utf-8">
  <title>Menu</title>
  <style>
    .sidebar { float: left; width: 300px; }
    @media (max-width: 600px) {
      .sidebar { float: none; width: auto; }
    }
  </style>
</head>

options.text: A media type: the query has to be written `@media screen and (max-width: 600px)` to apply on phones
options.why: The media type is optional. `@media (max-width: 600px)` applies to every media type, phones included. The query fails because the width it measures is not 390px.

options.text: A larger breakpoint: media queries measure device pixels, so a 390px phone with a 3x screen is 1170px wide
options.why: Media queries use CSS pixels, not physical device pixels, so the screen's pixel density doesn't matter. Raising the breakpoint to about 1200px would also switch many desktop windows to the mobile layout and hide the real problem: the layout viewport is too wide.

options.text: An external stylesheet: mobile browsers apply media queries only from a `<link>` file, not from a `<style>` block
options.why: Media queries work the same in `<style>` blocks, external stylesheets and `<link media="...">` attributes, on desktop and mobile alike.

explanation:
Without a viewport meta tag, mobile browsers assume the page was designed for desktop. They lay it out in a virtual **layout viewport** that is much wider than the screen (typically around 980px), then zoom out so the whole thing fits. The media query asks whether the viewport is at most 600px wide, and 980px is not, so the desktop layout is used and shrunk down.

```html
<meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1">
```

- `width=device-width` makes the layout viewport as wide as the device in CSS pixels (about 390px here), so `(max-width: 600px)` matches.
- `initial-scale=1` starts the page at 100% zoom instead of zoomed out.

Avoid adding `maximum-scale=1` or `user-scalable=no`: they block pinch-zoom, which people with low vision rely on.

question: A content style guide asks for the most fitting element for each highlighted phrase below. Which mapping matches the meanings the HTML spec gives these elements?

snippets.code:
1. "Warning: do not unplug the device during the update."
   (the warning)
2. "I didn't SAY she stole it."
   (spoken stress on "say", which changes the meaning)
3. "We crossed the Atlantic on the Queen Mary."
   (a ship's name)
4. "The Lumen X2 has a 40-hour battery."
   (product name highlighted in a review, no extra importance)

options.why: This treats `<b>` and `<i>` as deprecated presentational tags. They aren't deprecated: HTML gives them their own meanings. A ship name isn't stressed speech, and a product name in a review isn't more important than the text around it, so `<em>` and `<strong>` would add meaning that isn't there.

`<strong>` and `<em>` are swapped. `<em>` is **stress emphasis**, the kind of stress that changes what a sentence means when spoken. `<strong>` marks **importance, seriousness or urgency**, which fits a warning.

This picks elements by their default look. `<b>` and `<i>` only set text apart; they don't say it's important or stressed. The warning's urgency and the spoken stress are part of the meaning, so they need `<strong>` and `<em>`.

explanation:
By default the pairs look the same (`<b>` and `<strong>` both compute to `font-weight: 700`; `<i>` and `<em>` are both italic), so choose by meaning and style with CSS:

- `<strong>`: strong **importance, seriousness or urgency** (warnings, critical steps).
- `<em>`: **stress emphasis**; moving it to another word changes the meaning of the sentence.
- `<i>`: text in an **alternate voice or mood** with no extra emphasis: technical terms, idiomatic phrases from another language, taxonomic names, thoughts, ship names.
- `<b>`: text you want to **draw attention to** without extra importance: keywords in a summary, product names in a review, an article lede.

If you only want bold or italic for visual reasons (a heading style, a quote), use CSS (`font-weight`, `font-style`) on a `<span>` or the relevant element instead of any of the four.

options.why: Character references are decoded while parsing, in attribute values as well as in text. The attribute's stored value is `Fish & Chips <3`, and `getAttribute` returns it as is.

`innerHTML` doesn't return the stored text; it serializes the element's children back to HTML. While serializing text, it escapes `&`, `<` and `>` again so the output can be parsed back to the same DOM.

explanation:
The parser decodes character references (`&`, `<`, ...) in **both** text and attribute values. The DOM stores the actual characters: the attribute value and the text node both hold `Fish & Chips <3`.

- In source HTML, write `&` for a literal ampersand and `<` for `<` in text. Inside a double-quoted attribute, also escape `"` as `"`.
- When setting values from JavaScript, don't escape anything yourself: `setAttribute('title', 'Fish & Chips')` and `textContent = '<3'` store the text exactly. Escaping is only needed when you build HTML strings, which is why `textContent` is the safe choice for untrusted text.
